newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamists confident of poll prospects.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamists confident of poll prospects.

text.p: Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, his coalition deteriorating by the day, warned secularist critics on Monday that his Islam-based Welfare Party would emerge stronger than ever from any fresh elections.

As pressure mounted on Erbakan to step down at once to make way for an "election" government, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader said Welfare was poised to collect 10 million votes -- up from a slim plurality of about six million in 1995.
And he vowed that overwhelmingly-Moslem Turkey without Welfare at its head could never be truly democratic.
"We got some six million votes last time. If we had an election now we would get at least 10 million," Erbakan told foreign correspondents at a rare briefing.
"If there is going to be democracy in Turkey, the backbone must be the Welfare Party...Seventy million people are confident about our honesty and sincerity."

Erbakan fired off the first round of his unofficial election campaign as his putative partners, the pro-Western True Path Party, pushed him to implement an earlier agreement and hand over power to True Path leader Tansu Ciller.

"In the next one or two days, the 54th government will come to an end, Erbakan will resign. In such an environment, the thing to do is to form an election government," Ciller told a group of business leaders in the capital Ankara.
However, political analysts said Erbakan might insist on a firm election date, probably in October or November, before he would surrender power voluntarily to his rival-turned-partner.
A Welfare spokesman said the party had agreed to hand power to Ciller this week, but at a price.
"We have reached an agreement to leave office on June 18. There are, of course, conditions," spokesman Oguzhan Asilturk told a news conference. He did not specify the conditions.

Erbakan, ruling in coalition with True Path, is locked in an increasingly nasty battle with the secularist establishment over what it says is a government-fostered rise in Moslem activism. The proposed power swap is designed to ease that pressure.

The mainstream media is filled with near-hysteria over perceived threats to the official secular order, while Turkey's highest court is weighing charges that could close down Welfare altogether as "unconstitutional".

The restive armed forces, who have deposed three civilian governments in four decades, have made no effort to hide their displeasure with the Islamists. Last week, they threatened to use "force of arms" to defend their secular ideals.

Already, True Path has been hit by enough defections to cost the government its majority in parliament, limiting Erbakan's room to manoeuvre and raising the prospects for early polls, perhaps by autumn.
However, the prime minister himself has doggedly declined to fix a date for any handover of power.

"The government protocol envisages that after one year the prime minister can be changed after considering the situation," Erbakan told the news briefing in response to persistent questions on whether he was to stand down.
"It is not very important who has what position. Whenever we have to do something together, we shall do it together."
All the same, Erbakan and his senior aides appear confident that polls would only strengthen their hands in the struggle with the traditional ruling elite, spearheaded by the army.
"Definitely, we are going to win the next elections," Abdullah Gul, minister of state and close Erbakan confidante, told reporters ahead of the prime minister's news conference.
In fact, Erbakan devoted much of his lengthy opening remarks to highlighting what he said were the achievements of the coalition's 12 months in power.

He said corruption in big public contracts had been largely eliminated, local Welfare adminstrations were flourishing and chaotic public finances were being put right -- at least until what he termed the "artificial crisis" with the army had undermined his rule.
The result was a rising Welfare tide that could not be stemmed by outlawing the party or demonising its leaders.
"You simply cannot consider that a big portion of the population has ceased to exist. Members of the party will have to express their beliefs," he said.
